01 Independent · Data analysis · 2026

Netflix Went Global.
Did Its Catalogue?

Between 2016 and 2019 Netflix added five times more titles a year, so I asked whether that growth changed what it added: more TV shows, more international productions, newer releases? I analysed 5,884 titles from the Kaggle Netflix dataset, testing each idea with chi-square, Kruskal–Wallis and logistic regression. Two of the three predictions were not supported. TV's share showed no steady trend, and non-US additions rose to 61% in 2018 before falling back to 52%. Additions actually got older, with the share released within a year falling from 65% to 53%. The data is a January 2020 snapshot, so titles removed before then are missing, a limitation the write-up spells out.

02 Independent · Data analysis · 2026

What Makes a
Movie Popular?

Is a film's popularity explained by its genre, how recent it is, or how well it's rated? I first cleaned and visualised 9,800 popular films from TMDB, then went back and audited my own notebook. That audit found four issues, including a binning step that silently dropped the 100 lowest-rated films. The corrected analysis shows recency matters most among the three: median popularity jumps from 22 for 2010s films to 35 for the 2020s. Rating barely matters (Spearman ρ = 0.13), and Drama is the most common genre but one of the least popular. Even together, genre, recency, rating and vote count explain only 30% of popularity.

03 Independent · Data analysis · 2026

Can Countries Grow
While Cutting Emissions?

Which countries grew their economies while cutting CO₂ between 2005 and 2019, and does that hold once emissions in imported goods are counted? Using Our World in Data's emissions and GDP data for 117 countries, I classified each on territorial and consumption-based emissions. 26 countries, including the UK, Germany and the US, decoupled on both. Counting imports shrank the list from 34 to 28: Switzerland's territorial emissions fell 20%, but its consumption emissions rose 12%. Decoupling was overwhelmingly a rich-country result, reached by 62% of the richest third and none of the poorest. Consumption figures are modelled estimates, which the write-up flags.

04 Independent · Data analysis · 2026

Smoking, BMI and
Medical Costs

How much more are smokers charged for medical care, and is the penalty the same for everyone? Using the Kaggle medical cost dataset of 1,337 adults, I fitted regression models adjusting for age, sex, children and region, and checked them with 2,000 bootstrap resamples. Smokers' median charges were 4.7 times non-smokers'. The penalty more than doubled above BMI 30, from about $13,400 to $33,200 a year, while BMI made almost no difference for non-smokers. Adding that interaction raised the model's explained variation from 75% to 86%. The dataset is simulated from census figures, so these are patterns in the data, not real-world causes.

05 Independent · Machine learning · 2026

Predicting
Customer Churn

Which customers are about to leave, and can a simple model find them in time? Using IBM's Telco Customer Churn data of 7,043 customers, I compared logistic regression with gradient boosting under cross-validation and a held-out test set. Churn was 43% on month-to-month contracts against 3% on two-year contracts, and 53% in a customer's first six months. The explainable logistic regression matched the more complex model (test ROC-AUC 0.85 vs 0.84) and was well calibrated. Contacting the riskiest 20% of customers would reach half of those who leave, 2.5 times better than random. It's a sample dataset, and the results show association rather than cause.

06 Academic · MSc coursework, refactored · 2026

ICO Fundraising
Prediction

Which token sales reach their fundraising target? I modelled Initial Coin Offering outcomes from digital-presence, compliance and geographic signals in R. The data was sparse and patchily reported, so careful imputation and strict leakage and class-imbalance controls mattered more than the choice of model. I later refactored my own coursework script into a tested pipeline. That rebuild caught a leak in the original, where KNN had been tuned on the test set. 34 automated checks now run on every change.

07 Academic · Undergraduate project · 2024

Customer Lifetime
Value Prediction

Which customers are worth the most over time? I modelled purchasing behaviour across 10,000+ transaction records to find high-value segments. The lift came from better features, not a bigger model. Feature engineering improved predictive performance by 22% over the baseline, measured with cross-validation. The results became retention and growth recommendations. The work contributed to a peer-reviewed paper in IJRAR (2024).

01 Hackathon · Solo · In Development

AI Research
Assistant

A solo entry to the Nebius × NVIDIA Global AI Hackathon 2026, due 30 October 2026. The idea is a research assistant that shows its working: it plans a question, finds sources, weighs the evidence and answers with citations you can check. It should also flag unsupported claims and compare conflicting evidence. The intended stack is NVIDIA open-source models through Nebius Token Factory or Nebius AI Cloud. It is in concept and development planning, so nothing has been built or submitted yet. Links and the full story will follow once it is.

02 Hackathon · Team participant · Completed · October 2026

ResultWise

Built with a team of four at the AI in Healthcare Hackathon, Leeds, on 24–25 October 2026. Scan follow-ups can slip through the gap when care moves between hospitals, because each system sees only its own bookings. ResultWise uses AI to read breast cancer scan reports, plain rules to track bookings at both hospitals, and a clinician to approve every message before it reaches the patient in her own language. I set up the repository, built the first working prototype, the clinician review flow and the evaluation, and maintained the web app the team demoed. On 10 held-out synthetic reports the AI found every follow-up, while keyword rules found 22%. It is a prototype on synthetic data, not clinically validated or deployed.

03 Hackathon · Top 10 finalist · Oct 2025 · Rebuilt 2026, in active development

Hauntify

Built for a Halloween hackathon in October 2025 and selected as a Top 10 finalist. Hauntify is a Streamlit app that mixes computer vision and NLP. Snap a webcam photo and turn it Vampire, Ghost, Zombie or Witch with OpenCV effects. Type a sentence and a small text classifier scores how spooky it is, then suggests a costume. The text model reached about 90% accuracy. It has since been rebuilt as a live web app with face-tracking filters and three Halloween mini-games.

01 Research · Ongoing · University of Leeds

Machine Learning for Hidden Grip Strategies in Human Reach-to-Grasp Movements

How a hand reaches and closes may carry a trace of what the eyes could see. This work continues my MSc dissertation with Dr Carlo Campagnoli and Dr Elham Mirfarah at the University of Leeds. The dissertation used two experimental datasets, participant-independent evaluation and both the grasp and transport parts of the movement. Discussions with Dr Campagnoli have identified potential for a paper, starting with a matched analysis across both experiments and movement components. Longer term, I want to explore whether these measurements could support research on stroke-related visuomotor difficulties. That direction is exploratory: no patient study is underway, and the paper has not yet been submitted.

02 MSc Dissertation · University of Leeds · Completed

Machine Learning
× Human Movement

Can a model tell what someone could see from the way they reach? I analysed 2,600+ trials from 23 participants across two motion-capture experiments, owning the grasp stream of a two-stream project. Logistic Regression and Random Forest were tested on people the model had never seen, with permutation tests to rule out chance; deep sequence models were explored separately. The signal was statistically significant but modest. The simplest model won, with Logistic Regression reaching 64.2%. Supervised by Dr Carlo Campagnoli and Dr Elham Mirfarah, and submitted in September 2026.

03 Clinical Research · Proposal Stage

Visuomotor Control
After Stroke

What might the same movement measurements reveal after a stroke? This proposal would compare reaching and grasping between stroke survivors and healthy adults under limited visual feedback. It looks at velocity, smoothness, coordination and movement time. Those measures would be related to established clinical assessments. The long-term aim is to inform understanding of motor impairment and recovery. It is an early-stage proposal awaiting academic feedback, not completed research.

06 — About

Point of view.

"I don't just train models.I question what the data is actually telling us."

DATA× HUMAN BEHAVIOUR× AI× PRODUCT

I hold an MSc in Data Science and Analytics from the University of Leeds, built on a B.Tech in Information Technology. I work where machine learning, statistical rigour and product thinking meet: as curious about why a model works as whether it does, and about what a result means for the person who has to act on it.

The habit is simple: interpretable features before complexity, validation honest enough to trust, and findings a non-technical stakeholder can act on. Human movement, customer behaviour, hospital reports. Different data, same discipline.

Right now: building an agentic personal assistant that coordinates tasks, analyses information and supports decisions.
